content: Systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) is a condition characterized by a state of inflammation affecting the entire body, or system, without a confirmed source of infection. It is considered a serious medical condition that requires prompt attention. The criteria for diagnosing SIRS were established in 1992. To meet the criteria for SIRS, a patient must exhibit at least two of the following clinical findings: A body temperature that is either elevated above 38°C (100.4°F) or decreased below 36°C (96.8°F). A heart rate exceeding 90 beats per minute (tachycardia). A respiratory rate greater than 20 breaths per minute (tachypnea) or, alternatively, a partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PaCO2) in arterial blood less than 32 mmHg. An abnormal white blood cell count, either elevated above 12,000 cells/mm³, decreased below 4,000 cells/mm³, or with more than 10% immature white blood cells (band forms), a condition known as bandemia. The distinction between SIRS and sepsis lies in the presence of infection. When SIRS occurs in the context of a suspected or confirmed infection, it is referred to as sepsis. SIRS can lead to severe complications, including multiple organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS), which is a life-threatening condition involving the failure of multiple organ systems. The causes of SIRS are varied and include: Severe trauma Postoperative complications Burns Acute pancreatitis Immunodeficiency states, such as those seen in AIDS SIRS is also related to the concept of a cytokine storm, which refers to a dysregulated and excessive release of cytokines. While the term cytokine storm is not commonly used in clinical medicine, SIRS can be considered a subset of this phenomenon, as it involves a similar dysregulation of the immune response.
